title: Boss: The Collector
summary: Four challenges where the hard part is choosing the right collection, then writing the method around it.

steps.title: Pick the right container
body: Every trial here is solved with methods and collections you already know. Before you type, ask one question: **what do I need to remember, and how will I look it up?**
- By position, in order: an array or a `List<T>`.
- By a name or other key: a `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`.
- Only *have I seen this before?*: a `HashSet<T>`.
Sometimes the answer is two of them working together.

steps.title: Trial 1: Vital statistics
prompt: Write three methods that each take an `int[]`. You may assume the array is never empty.
- `int Min(int[] values)` returns the smallest value.
- `int Max(int[] values)` returns the largest value.
- `double Average(int[] values)` returns the mean, with its decimals.
For `{ 4, 9, 2 }` they return `2`, `9` and `5.0`. For `{ 1, 2 }` the average is `1.5`.
Write the loops yourself: the built-in `.Min()`, `.Max()`, `.Average()` and `.Sum()` are off limits.

forbid.message: Does not call the built-in .Min(), .Max(), .Average() or .Sum()

hints: `Min` and `Max` are the "best so far" pattern. Start with `values[0]`, not with 0: the array might hold only negative numbers.
For `Average`, add everything up in an `int total`, then divide by `values.Length`.
An int divided by an int drops the decimals. Convert one side first: `(double)total / values.Length`.

steps.title: Trial 2: No repeats
prompt: Write a method `List<int> Unique(int[] items)` that returns the items with the duplicates removed. Each value appears once, at the position of its **first** appearance.
starter: // add each item the first time you meet it
template: Dojo.Eq("Unique of { 3, 1, 3, 2, 1 } is [3, 1, 2]", new List<int> { 3, 1, 2 }, Unique(new[] { 3, 1, 3, 2, 1 }));
Dojo.Eq("Unique of { 5, 5, 5, 5 } is [5]", new List<int> { 5 }, Unique(new[] { 5, 5, 5, 5 }));
Dojo.Eq("Unique of { 9, 8, 7 } is [9, 8, 7]", new List<int> { 9, 8, 7 }, Unique(new[] { 9, 8, 7 }));
Dojo.Eq("Unique of an empty array is empty", new List<int>(), Unique(new int[0]));
hints: Walk the items in order. Add an item to `result` only if you have not met it before.
The simple test is `!result.Contains(item)`. It works, but it searches the whole list every time.
Faster: keep a `HashSet<int> seen` next to the list. `seen.Add(item)` returns `true` only the first time, so `if (seen.Add(item)) result.Add(item);` does the whole job.

steps.title: Trial 3: Word frequency
prompt: Read words, one per line, until the line `end`. Count how often each word appears, treating upper and lower case as the same word (`text.ToLower()` gives you the lowercase version of a string).
- one line per word, in lowercase, **in the order the words first appeared**: `word: count`
- a last line naming the most common word. If several share the top count, name the one that appeared first.
You may assume there is at least one word before `end`.
starter: // A dictionary does not promise to remember the order things were added.
// What else could you keep to remember it?
// 2. print each word with its count, in first-seen order

tests.name: mixed case words
tests.stdin:
the
cat
The
mat
THE
cat
end
tests.expect:
the: 3
cat: 2
mat: 1
Most common: the

tests.name: the most common word is not the first
tests.stdin:
zebra
apple
Mango
apple
mango
Apple
end
tests.expect:
zebra: 1
apple: 3
mango: 2
Most common: apple

tests.name: a tie goes to the word seen first

hints: Lowercase each line as you read it, then use the counting pattern: `ContainsKey`, then `++` or `= 1`.
Keep a `List<string> order` beside the dictionary. Add a word to it only the first time you see it. Printing is then a `foreach` over `order`, reading each count from the dictionary.
For the most common word, track `best` and `bestCount` while you walk `order`. Update them only when a count is strictly greater (`>`), so that on a tie the earlier word keeps its place.

steps.title: Trial 4: The stockroom
prompt: Run a stockroom from commands, one per line. The starter already reads each line and splits it into words for you.
| `add NAME N` | Adds `N` of the item to the stock. Prints nothing. |
| `remove NAME N` | Takes `N` away. If the item is not stocked, or there are fewer than `N`, change nothing and print `Cannot remove NAME`. An item that drops to 0 leaves the stockroom entirely. |
| `count NAME` | Prints `NAME: N`, with `0` for an item that is not stocked. |
| `report` | Prints every stocked item as `NAME: N`, in alphabetical order. Prints `Empty` when there is nothing. |
starter: // Split cuts the line at each space:
// handle add, remove, count and report here
solution: if (!stock.TryGetValue(name, out int have) || have < amount)

tests.name: the example
tests.stdin:
add pear 2
add apple 5
remove apple 1
remove pear 3
count kiwi
report
end
tests.expect:
Cannot remove pear
kiwi: 0
apple: 4
pear: 2

tests.name: adding twice accumulates
tests.stdin:
add apple 3
add pear 2
add apple 4
count apple
count pear
end

tests.name: removing too many, or something unknown
tests.stdin:
add nut 5
remove nut 2
count nut
remove nut 9
remove fig 1
count nut
end
tests.expect:
nut: 3
Cannot remove nut
Cannot remove fig
nut: 3

tests.name: an item at 0 leaves the report
tests.stdin:
report
add pear 2
add apple 1
add melon 6
remove apple 1
report
count apple
remove pear 2
remove melon 6
report
end

hints: `stock` maps an item name to how many there are. Branch on `command` with a `switch` or an `if`/`else if` chain. The name is `parts[1]` and the amount is `int.Parse(parts[2])`.

`stock.TryGetValue(name, out int have)` gives you the current amount, and leaves `have` at 0 when the item is missing. That covers `count` directly, and it is the first half of `add` and `remove`. Delete an emptied item with `stock.Remove(name)`.
For `report`, a dictionary has no order of its own. Copy the keys into a list with `new List<string>(stock.Keys)`, call `Sort()`, then `foreach` over the list and print `stock[name]` for each.

steps.title: Trial 5: Sidekick's inbox
prompt: **Sidekick piece. Milestone: sk runs.** This is the brain of `sk shell`. Your `RunShell` from Control flow reads commands, and your `AddTitle` from this module adds titles once; this method decides what each command does. Both are ready to call. When you pass, `sk shell` is a working inbox on your own machine.
Write `static string Inbox(List<string> open, List<string> done, string line)`. Trim the line; the first word (lowercased) is the command, the rest (trimmed) is its argument. Return the reply:
| `list` | nothing | `1. <first>`, `2. <second>`, ... one per line (joined with `\n`); `Inbox zero. Nice.` when `open` is empty |
| `done <n>` | moves item n (1-based) from `open` to the end of `done` | `Done: <title> (<count of done> done)` |
| `done`/`drop` with a bad number | nothing | `No item <argument>. Try: list` |
| anything else | nothing | `Unknown command: <command>. Try add, list, done, drop` |
The tests also run your Inbox inside your own `RunShell`, exactly as `sk shell` does.
starter: static string Inbox(List<string> open, List<string> done, string line)
// split into the command and the rest, then switch on the command
solution: static string Inbox(List<string> open, List<string> done, string line)
for (int i = 0; i < open.Count; i++) lines.Add($"{i + 1}. {open[i]}");
if (!int.TryParse(rest, out int n) || n < 1 || n > open.Count) return $"No item {rest}. Try: list";
return $"Unknown command: {verb}. Try add, list, done, drop";
template: var dojoOpen = new List<string> { "Fix login", "Write docs" };
Dojo.Eq("list numbers the items", "1. Fix login\n2. Write docs", Inbox(dojoOpen, dojoDone, "list"));
Dojo.Eq("add a new title", "Added: Plan demo", Inbox(dojoOpen, dojoDone, "add Plan demo"));
Dojo.Eq("the title is in the list", 3, dojoOpen.Count);
Dojo.Eq("a duplicate is refused, command in capitals", "Already there: fix login", Inbox(dojoOpen, dojoDone, "ADD fix login"));
Dojo.Eq("add with no title", "Usage: add <title>", Inbox(dojoOpen, dojoDone, "add"));
Dojo.Eq("done moves an item", "Done: Fix login (1 done)", Inbox(dojoOpen, dojoDone, "done 1"));
Dojo.Eq("done removed it from open", "Write docs", dojoOpen[0]);
Dojo.Eq("done added it to done", new List<string> { "Fix login" }, dojoDone);
Dojo.Eq("drop removes an item", "Dropped: Plan demo", Inbox(dojoOpen, dojoDone, "drop 2"));
Dojo.Eq("dropped items are not done", 1, dojoDone.Count);
Dojo.Eq("done with a number too big", "No item 9. Try: list", Inbox(dojoOpen, dojoDone, "done 9"));
Dojo.Eq("done with zero", "No item 0. Try: list", Inbox(dojoOpen, dojoDone, "done 0"));
Dojo.Eq("drop with no number", "No item x. Try: list", Inbox(dojoOpen, dojoDone, "drop x"));
Dojo.Eq("spaces around the line", "1. Write docs", Inbox(dojoOpen, dojoDone, "  list  "));
Dojo.Eq("an unknown command", "Unknown command: dance. Try add, list, done, drop", Inbox(dojoOpen, dojoDone, "dance"));
Dojo.Eq("an empty inbox", "Inbox zero. Nice.", Inbox(new List<string>(), new List<string>(), "list"));

Dojo.Eq("sk shell: your RunShell around your Inbox", "sk> Added: Buy milk
sk> 1. Buy milk
sk> Done: Buy milk (1 done)
sk> Inbox zero. Nice.
sk> Bye. Go build something.",
internal static void RunShell(Func<string, string> run)
internal static bool AddTitle(List<string> titles, string title)
hints: Split once: `int space = trimmed.IndexOf(' ');` The command is everything before it (or the whole line), the argument everything after it, trimmed.

A `switch (verb)` with a `case` per command. `case "done": case "drop":` can share one block: parse the number with `int.TryParse`, check `1 <= n <= open.Count`, take `open[n - 1]` and `open.RemoveAt(n - 1)`.
`list` builds a `List<string>` of `$"{i + 1}. {open[i]}"` lines and returns `string.Join("\n", lines)`.
steps.explain: This is what a command-line app is: a loop that reads a line (`RunShell`) and a method that turns a line into an answer (`Inbox`). Keeping them apart is why each could be tested on its own.
steps.stdin:
add Buy milk
list
done 1
list
quit

build.unlocks: Milestone: `sk shell` runs a real inbox. Sidekick runs!
